title: Volume Profile Anatomy: POC, Value Area, HVN & LVN

lessons.title: How a volume profile is built
lessons.desc: Pick one ES session and look at it as a candlestick chart and as a session volume profile side by side. Find two candles whose range overlaps the POC row, and check that most of the session's heavy trading sits in that band.
lessons.descHtml: Pick one ES session and look at it as a candlestick chart and as a session volume profile side by side. Find two candles whose range overlaps the POC row, and check that most of the session's heavy trading sits in that band.

lessons.title: Finding the POC, VAH and VAL
lessons.desc: For the last three sessions, write down the POC, VAH and VAL before the next session opens. Next day, note which of the three levels price touched first and what it did there. Record only what happened, not what you expected.

lessons.title: Computing a value area by hand
lessons.desc: Take the worked table in this chapter and redo it on real data from your platform: copy ten to fifteen rows of volume around the POC, apply the two-row method, and compare your VAH and VAL with the platform's. Explain any one-tick difference.

lessons.title: Spotting HVNs and LVNs
lessons.desc: On a five-day composite profile, circle every HVN and LVN. Then scroll forward and tag each LVN crossing as "fast" (one or two bars) or "slow". This builds your own evidence on how LVNs behave on your instrument.

lessons.title: Volume vs TPO profiles
lessons.desc: Put a TPO profile and a volume profile on the same session. Find one price where they disagree most, then check the time and sales or a 1-minute chart for what happened there, for example a news release.

bodyHtml:
A candlestick chart tells you when price moved. A volume profile tells you where business was done. It takes all the contracts traded over a period and stacks them sideways at each price, so you can see at a glance which prices the market accepted and which it rushed past. This chapter builds a profile from scratch, then names its parts: the point of control, the value area and its edges, and the high- and low-volume nodes. You will compute a value area by hand, because doing it once makes every profile you see afterwards easier to read.

Volume profile grew out of the Market Profile work that J. Peter Steidlmayer developed at the Chicago Board of Trade, which the exchange released to the public in 1985 (covered in VP-02). Treat everything here as a method traders use to organise information, not as a law of how price must behave.

How a volume profile is built

Volume is the number of contracts that changed hands. A volume profile answers one question for every price level: how many contracts traded here during the period I picked? Stack those totals horizontally and you get a histogram standing on its side. Long bars are prices where a lot of trading happened. Short bars are prices the market visited only briefly.

There are two ways platforms build it. The precise way uses every individual trade (tick data): each trade adds its size to the row for its exact price. The approximate way uses lower-timeframe bars. TradingView, for example, says in its help pages that it builds a daily session profile by loading the session's 1-minute bars and spreading each bar's volume across the prices that bar covered. The approximate way is usually close enough to read the shape. It can be off by a tick or two on exact levels.

The row size (also called ticks per row) matters. On E-mini S&P 500 futures (ES) the minimum price move is 0.25 index points, so the finest profile has one row per 0.25. Wider rows smooth the shape. Narrower rows show more detail and more noise. Pick one setting per instrument and keep it, so your levels are comparable from day to day.

The point of control (POC)

The point of control is the single price with the most volume in the profile. TradingView defines it the same way: the price level with the highest traded volume for the period. In the session below the POC is 5,211.75, with 1,420 contracts out of 9,450.

Traders read the POC as the price the market treated as fairest during that period, because it is where buyers and sellers were most willing to trade with each other. It is a reference, not a wall. Price often returns to it, trades through it, or ignores it completely, depending on what happens next.

The value area, VAH and VAL

The value area is the range of prices around the POC that contains a set share of the period's volume. The convention is 70%. It comes from the original CBOT Market Profile, which borrowed the idea that about 70% of a normal distribution sits within one standard deviation of the middle. TradingView's documentation gives 70% as the typical setting, and Sierra Chart lets you change it. The top of the range is the value area high (VAH). The bottom is the value area low (VAL).

The 70% is a convention, not something the market knows about. Treat VAH and VAL as the edges of where most business was done, and expect different platforms to disagree by a tick when they use different methods or row sizes.

Worked example: computing the value area by hand

The most common method is the two-row method from the CBOT Market Profile material. Start at the POC. Look at the next two rows above and add their volumes. Look at the next two rows below and add theirs. Include whichever pair is larger. Repeat until the included volume reaches 70% of the total. Here it is on the illustrative session above (9,450 contracts, so the target is 6,615).

StepAddNext 2 aboveNext 2 belowTotal so far
0POC 5,211.75--1,420 (15.0%)
1add below1,8802,2003,620 (38.3%)
2add above1,8801,3005,500 (58.2%)
3add below6201,3006,800 (72.0%)

The procedure stops once the running total passes 70%. It ends at 72.0%, because it adds two rows at a time and overshoots slightly. The value area runs from 5,210.75 (VAL) to 5,212.25 (VAH). Notice that it is not centred on the POC. Volume below the POC was heavier, so the value area grew downward faster than upward. That lopsidedness is information: it tells you on which side of the POC more business was done.

Try it yourself

Change the rule to one row at a time and redo the table. You will usually land on the same area, or one row different. That difference is exactly why two platforms can show VAH or VAL a tick apart.

High-volume and low-volume nodes (HVN and LVN)

Most profiles are not one smooth hill. They have bulges and pinches. A high-volume node (HVN) is a bulge: a cluster of prices where a lot of volume traded, usually around a POC. A low-volume node (LVN) is a pinch: a thin area between bulges where little volume traded. In our session the main HVN sits around the POC, a smaller HVN forms at 5,213.25, and the LVN at 5,212.75 separates them. Sierra Chart calls these "peaks and valleys" in its Volume by Price study.

The common reading is simple. An HVN is a price area the market accepted, so price tends to slow down and rotate there. An LVN is a price area the market rejected, or moved through quickly, so price tends to move fast through it and the far edge of the LVN often acts as a reaction point. These are tendencies traders watch for, not rules.

This links directly to what you already know from the core course. A thin LVN is the profile's version of an imbalance, much like a fair value gap on a candle chart (chapter 10), and VP-11 shows how to combine them.

Volume profile vs TPO profile

You will see two kinds of profile. A volume profile counts contracts. A TPO profile (time price opportunity, from Market Profile) counts how many 30-minute periods visited each price. They usually look similar, because price that spends a long time somewhere tends to trade a lot there. They differ when a large amount of volume trades in a short burst, for example at a news release. The volume profile then shows a big node where the TPO profile shows very little.

Many traders keep both on screen and treat the disagreement as useful: heavy volume in little time can mean a large participant did business quickly at that price.

Common mistakes

  • Treating the POC as support or resistance by itself. It is a reference for where value was, not a promise that price will bounce there.
  • Mixing row sizes. A profile with 1-point rows and one with 0.25-point rows give different POCs. Keep settings fixed per instrument.
  • Using a profile from the wrong period. A profile built on the visible chart changes every time you scroll. Anchor it to something definite, like a session or a swing (see VP-05).
  • Reading tick volume as traded volume. On spot FX and CFDs, TradingView counts price updates, not contracts. The profile shape can still be useful, but it is a different measure (see VP-10).
  • Expecting every platform to agree to the tick. The value area method, the row size and whether the profile is built from ticks or bars all shift the edges slightly.

Key takeaways

  • A volume profile shows how many contracts traded at each price over a period you choose.
  • The POC is the price with the most volume. The value area holds 70% of the volume by convention, bounded by VAH and VAL.
  • The two-row method starts at the POC and adds the heavier pair of rows until it reaches 70%.
  • HVNs are accepted areas where price tends to rotate. LVNs are thin areas price tends to cross quickly.
  • These are reading tools, not predictions. Always combine them with structure and risk rules.

Practice exercises

  1. Open an ES or NQ chart and add a session volume profile to yesterday's regular trading hours. Write down the POC, VAH and VAL before you look at today's price.
  2. Copy the volumes of the ten rows around a POC into a spreadsheet. Compute the 70% value area with the two-row method and compare it with your platform's VAH and VAL.
  3. Mark every LVN on the last five session profiles. For each one, note whether price later crossed it in one or two bars or stalled inside it. Keep the tally in your journal.
  4. Change the row size (for example 0.25, 1 and 2 points) on the same session and note how the POC moves. Choose a setting and record it in your playbook.

Self-check quiz

1. What does the point of control show?

The single price with the most traded volume in the period. It is a reference for where the market did the most business, not a guaranteed turning point.

2. Why is the value area set at 70%?

It is a convention from the original CBOT Market Profile, based on the share of a normal distribution within one standard deviation of the middle. Platforms let you change it.

3. In the two-row method, what do you compare at each step?

The combined volume of the next two rows above the current value area and the next two rows below it. You add the larger pair and repeat until you reach 70%.

4. Why was the value area in this chapter's example not centred on the POC?

More volume traded below the POC than above it, so the heavier pairs were on the lower side and the area grew downward.

5. How is an LVN usually read?

As a thin area the market moved through quickly or rejected, so price tends to cross it fast. The far side of it is often watched for a reaction.

6. Why might TradingView's profile on a forex CFD differ from a futures profile?

TradingView uses tick volume (the number of price updates) for forex and CFDs, not contracts traded, because spot FX has no single central exchange reporting volume.

Sources

  2. Volume by Price study - Sierra Chart documentation
  3. Market profile (history of the CBOT Market Profile and the 70% value area) - Wikipedia
  4. Micro E-mini Equity Index Futures FAQ (tick sizes and multipliers) - CME Group
  5. Mind Over Markets, Updated Edition (Dalton, Jones, Dalton; Wiley 2013) - further reading
  6. Markets and Market Logic (Steidlmayer, Koy; 1986) - further reading
